one_liner: Rust committing AEAD (ChaCha20 + keyed-BLAKE3 MAC); about 2x RustCrypto XChaCha20-Poly1305 and AES-256-GCM on 1-10 MB messages.
what_it_does: An authenticated cipher of the author's own design. A keyed-BLAKE3 KDF expands the key and a 24-byte nonce into a ChaCha20 key and 8-byte nonce plus a MAC key. The data is encrypted with the original DJB ChaCha20 (64-bit counter), then authenticated with keyed BLAKE3 over aad || len || ciphertext || len, producing a 32-byte tag. The API is its own and does not implement RustCrypto's aead traits: ChaCha20Blake3::new([u8; 32]), encrypt/decrypt returning Vec (needs the alloc feature), and no_std-friendly encrypt_in_place_detached/decrypt_in_place_detached. Its output does not interoperate with XChaCha20-Poly1305 or AES-GCM.
how_it_is_fast: The bundled `chacha` crate computes ChaCha blocks in a word-sliced (one block per SIMD lane) layout: 16 blocks per iteration with AVX-512 (_mm512_rol_epi32 rotates), 8 with AVX2, and 4 with NEON or WASM simd128. A scalar fallback covers inputs under 128 bytes and machines without SIMD. Authentication uses the blake3 crate, whose x86_64 build defaults to hand-written SSE4.1/AVX2/AVX-512 assembly (NEON C intrinsics on aarch64), so the MAC also scales with vector width. In the author's table the RustCrypto baselines plateau near 1.5-1.7 GB/s from 64 KB up while this construction reaches 3.3 GB/s. A per-message BLAKE3 KDF call plus a MAC finalization makes it slower than both baselines at 64 B-1 KB.
when_to_use: Rust code encrypting large one-shot buffers (64 KB and up, best at 1 MB and up), such as files, backups or object-storage blobs, where the author measured about 2x RustCrypto XChaCha20-Poly1305 and 2.2x RustCrypto AES-256-GCM.
Designs that use one long-lived key with random 24-byte nonces and want a committing AEAD; the README claims full context commitment.
Targets without AES hardware (microcontrollers, WASM with simd128, older ARM) when you control both ends of the channel and AES-GCM would be slow.
no_std builds: with default-features = false you still get the in-place detached API and compile-time SIMD selection.
when_not_to_use: Small messages. At 64 B-1 KB it is 1.1-1.5x slower than XChaCha20-Poly1305 and 2.5-5.2x slower than AES-256-GCM in the author's own table.

Interoperability or compliance needs (TLS, FIPS, JOSE/COSE). It is a non-standard construction specified only on the author's site, IANA/JOSE/COSE registration is still an open issue (#2), and the spec's KDF choice is questioned in open issue #11.

Portable x86-64 binaries built without -C target-cpu=native. The SIMD functions have no #[target_feature] attribute, and unmerged PR #12 reports about 55 MB/s instead of about 1.2 GB/s on an AVX2 i7-9750H as a result.
Streaming or larger-than-memory data. There is only a one-shot API (a streaming API is requested in open issue #1), and each call makes two passes over the buffer (encrypt, then MAC).
Machines with AES instructions where you just want the fastest AEAD. The AES-based siblings (AEGIS, HiAE, ROCCA-S) report tens to hundreds of Gbps, against about 3.3 GB/s here.

integration.form: crate (upstream recommends a git dependency on the main branch; the crates.io release is a third-party fork)
integration.dependencies: blake3 1.x (default features off, with neon and wasm32_simd; on x86_64 it builds hand-written assembly and on aarch64 the NEON code needs a C compiler), constant_time_eq 0.4, the in-repo `chacha` crate (path dependency), and optional zeroize 1.
integration.platforms: x86_64: AVX2/AVX-512 chosen by runtime detection with the std feature, or by compile-time target features in no_std builds. aarch64: NEON assumed. wasm32: simd128 at compile time only. Everything else uses the portable scalar fallback.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. ChaCha20Blake3 holds only the 32-byte key and every method takes &self, so one instance can be shared across threads; the inner ChaCha state is created per call.

gotchas: The crates.io crate chacha20-blake3 (0.9.11-0.10.0) is published by a third party from the paddor/chacha20-blake3 fork. That fork includes changes upstream has not merged: the target_feature fix, zeroization fixes, a Session API, and SSE2/AVX2 small-message paths. The upstream Cargo.toml is still at 0.9.11, so `cargo add` does not give you upstream.

Upstream's zeroize feature does not wipe everything. decrypt_in_place_detached never wipes kdf_out, Zeroizing::new(encryption_key).zeroize() wipes a copy of a Copy array, and the derived authentication-key copies are never wiped. The fork commit 'Zeroize all derived key material in AEAD' addresses this.

The tag is 32 bytes, 16 more than GCM or Poly1305. The Go port in skerkour/stdx-go (crypto/chacha20blake3) declares NonceSize = 32, while the Rust crate and that port's own error text say 24, so verify cross-language interop before you rely on it.

The maturity signals conflict. The author's January 2026 announcement title calls ChaCha20-BLAKE3 'stable and production-ready', but the bundled chacha crate's README says 'preliminary release, DO NOT USE IN PRODUCTION'. No third-party audit or cryptanalysis is documented.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over chacha20poly1305-simd when messages are large (64 KB and up), you want key commitment and random 24-byte nonces, and you do not need RFC 8439 wire compatibility; chacha20poly1305-simd is the better choice for small messages and standard ChaCha20-Poly1305. Over the AES-based siblings (libaegis, HiAE, ROCCA-S), pick it only when the target lacks AES instructions or you want one algorithm across microcontrollers, WASM and servers.
verified_claims_summary: The README table is first-party, single-core encryption on a virtualized AMD EPYC 9R45 (AWS ma8.xlarge), with no flags or rustc version stated; the repo's make bench target and .cargo/config.toml both use target-cpu=native. At 1-10 MB it measured 3,297-3,353 MB/s, against 1,654-1,664 MB/s for RustCrypto XChaCha20-Poly1305 and 1,476-1,477 MB/s for RustCrypto AES-256-GCM (0.11.0-rc.2 crates). It wins at 64 KB (2,153 vs 1,636 and 1,475 MB/s) and loses at 64 B and 1 KB. The shipped criterion bench covers only 64 B-64 KB with a 128-byte AAD, so the 1 MB and 10 MB rows cannot be reproduced from it. The AES-GCM arm runs without the aes crate's VAES cfgs, which open issue #4 argues understates AES-GCM on Zen CPUs.
status_note: The upstream repo is MIT-licensed with 103 stars; its last commit was 2026-01-15, and PR #12, the 2026-04 portable-build performance fix, has had no maintainer reply. The more recently updated crates.io release comes from a third-party fork, so 'active' is generous; pin a git revision or vendor the two small crates.
